title.en: Let the machine turn the knobs

after.en: You didn't design this kernel; it was learned from examples. This is how learned features replace hand-designed ones.

t.en: In <level-ref to="1-9"></level-ref> you looked at the input and output and worked out a 3×3 kernel cell by cell. Its numbers were tidy enough to guess. What if the nine numbers are a jumble with no pattern at all?

The new part is <part-ref to="part:learn3"></part-ref>: like the 3×3 kernel, it presses nine weights over the image, but you do not fill in the weights; it tunes them itself to match the tests' expected outputs. <level-ref to="4-2"></level-ref> had one or two knobs; this time there are nine.

Training first computes an output with the current parameters and compares it with the answer to obtain a loss. It then updates each parameter according to its effect on that loss. Here small changes estimate that effect; real neural networks usually use backpropagation to pass the effect of the loss backwards through the layers.

Real training often divides samples into mini-batches: one batch contributes to an update; one pass through the training set is an epoch. Batch size and the number of epochs are training choices, not weights learned by the network.
The input in this level is random noise, and the expected output is what you get by pressing some kernel nobody tells you about over it. Your task: make the output match the expected.

caption.en: Set 1: noise → after an unknown kernel is pressed over it

brief.en: In <level-ref to="4-2"></level-ref> you walked downhill with one knob, then two. This time it is an unknown 3×3 kernel: nine knobs with messy numbers you can't guess by eye. Wire up a learnable kernel and press "Train".

hint.en: Each press moves all nine knobs one step downhill together (just as in <level-ref to="4-1"></level-ref> and <level-ref to="4-2"></level-ref>, only with more knobs). Watch the loss curve go down.
